classification.difficultyReason: Separate two labelled groups to reveal outliers concealed by the pooled display, and explain the misconception.

inlines.text: The chart shows the masses, in kg, of some leopards.
Charlie says there are no outliers.

spec.sourceRegion: Question 2: leopard-mass chart to the right of the prompt
spec.description: Stacked-dot chart with a horizontal mass scale from 0 to 100, ticks and dashed vertical guides every 10, and a Female/Male legend below. Preserve the tall guide region above the dot stacks.
spec.mathematics: Female counts: 30 kg: 4; 40 kg: 5; 50 kg: 4; 80 kg: 1. Male counts: 20 kg: 1; 60 kg: 2; 70 kg: 5; 80 kg: 3; 90 kg: 1. There are 14 female and 12 male observations. At 80 kg, the female dot occupies the fourth position, above three male dots. No frequency axis is supplied.
spec.answerVisibility: All observations, scale labels and legend entries are permanent question givens. No outlier circles, labels or other answer annotations appear in the question chart.

answer.short: There appear to be no outliers when all leopards are put together, but there are outliers when females and males are considered separately: the 80 kg female and the 20 kg male.
answer.worked: The other females have masses from 30 kg to 50 kg, so the 80 kg female is unusually heavy. The other males have masses from 60 kg to 90 kg, so the 20 kg male is unusually light. Combining the groups conceals these outliers; each leopard should be compared with its own group.
